speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: There are a total of six sets of legislative changes contained in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This IIA scheme, which was introduced in 2012, was intended to incentivise manufacturers to adopt twin models of their operations between Singapore and Iskandar Malaysia in Johor, or the islands of Batam, Bintan and Karimun in Indonesia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: However, administrative complexities of tax computation in different jurisdictions made it challenging to operationalise the scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: As the IIA scheme was allowed to lapse after 31 December 2022, clause 16 deletes Part 9 of the Act to remove references to the IIA scheme while clause 19 provides for consequential amendments to the Income Tax Act 1947.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The second tax incentive scheme to be amended pertains to the Approved Foreign Loan (AFL) scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Second, new section 35(2) and (4) are inserted by clause 8 to enhance the powers of the Minister for Trade and Industry and the Minister for Finance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Today, an AFL incentive recipient incurs a debt payable to the Government if the recipient contravenes a condition of approval or section 34 by selling, transferring or disposing of equipment that was purchased and financed from an approved foreign loan without the Minister for Trade and Industry's permission.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This debt arises even when the company has already delivered its economic commitments as part of the AFL support or when the contraventions were unintentional or when any decision to sell, transfer or dispose of the equipment was reasonable and not of wilful intent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: With the new amendments, the Minister for Trade and Industry may decide whether to revoke the approval for the loan where any relevant contravention has taken place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: If the approval is revoked, a debt to the Government arises.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: But the Minister for Finance may waive the debt in whole or in part if the Minister for Finance is satisfied that the recipient did not knowingly or intentionally contravene the condition or section 34.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This legislative change allows debt liabilities to be imposed in a more targeted manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The third tax incentive scheme is the Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI) scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Under the agreement-based approach that was in place before 1 April 2023, companies were required to obtain the Economic Development Board (EDB)'s approval for every addition of an agreement or variation of an agreement in the ARI certificate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: However, as the use of intangible assets and intellectual property has become more pervasive, we need a more flexible approach to respond to companies' investment interests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Under the activity-based approach, the scope of the approved activity is specified in the certificate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Companies will enjoy tax exemptions or concessionary withholding tax rates for royalties, fees or contributions payable under all agreements entered into for the purpose of the approved activity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Companies will not need to undergo the onerous administrative process of seeking new approvals each time a new agreement is reached or an existing agreement is varied.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: To be clear, this is not a relaxation of the scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: We will still clearly define the activities which are supportable under the ARI incentive and companies that make claims under agreements which are not covered by a supportable activity will still have their claims rejected and must pay the full prevailing withholding tax.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Clauses 3 and 5 will effect the extension of the PC scheme while clause 6 will effect that of the DEI scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Both schemes remain relevant and effective in anchoring desired investments in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The fifth set of legislative amendments applies to the Investment Allowance (IA) scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The amendments to the IA scheme include (a) the extension of the IA scheme by five years for certain qualifying activities by clause 14(d) and 14(e); and (b) the removal of the qualifying activity of aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul services, given it has been assessed to be no longer relevant and the power to approve such projects lapsed in 2015.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Clauses 13, 14(a), 14(b) and 14(c) remove references to this qualifying activity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The last legislative amendment in clause 18 inserts a new section 61A to provide the Minister for Trade and Industry with retrospective revocation powers across all incentives under the Act in two scenarios.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The first scenario is the removal of any activity, agreement, arrangement, product or other matter from a certificate or letter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The second scenario is the revocation of any approval, certificate or letter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This amendment is aligned with the Income Tax Act 1947 and will allow the Government to respond proportionately when dealing with incentive breaches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: There is no impact on tax incentive recipients who meet their conditions and commitments.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: MNCs are an important part of a healthy economy, driving growth sectors and working in partnership with SMEs in their value chain to deliver value to the economy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The business community supports the Economic Expansion Incentives Scheme as this is an important aspect of our national strategy to attract and anchor MNCs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This change includes transitional provisions to facilitate a smooth transition to support the shift to the new scheme.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This amendment is a response to the evolving complexity of business structures, which necessitates a more dynamic and robust framework for managing tax incentives.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The new scheme simplifies the process for businesses to manage shared costs amongst various agreements and streamlines the administration of tax incentives by considering the operations of large companies that are engaged in multiple contracts for a fixed activity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, with the shift from an approval-centric system to an activity-centric system, it becomes essential to define what constitutes an approved activity more clearly.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Given the diverse and concurrent projects businesses often undertake, the Government could offer clear guidelines and examples of eligible activities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Providing this clarity will facilitate the application process, reduce duplications and lessen the need for handling exceptions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Shifting focus to a wider perspective, Singapore's dedication to fostering a favourable tax landscape for businesses remains steadfast.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This dedication is exemplified by the latest revision.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In the previous year, this Bill was amended to support companies undertaking emission reduction initiatives, encompassing investment in technology and equipment that contributes to quantifiable reductions in greenhouse gases.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This proactive change, spurred by feedback from the industry, underscores the significance of continual regulatory reviews.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In response to these changes, the Singapore Government has pledged to bolster non-tax benefits to preserve and enhance Singapore’s competitive appeal in a landscape that is rapidly evolving due to the new BEPS 2.0 norms.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: From a competitive vantage point, these incentives remain particularly crucial especially for certain mobile activities such as finance and research and development.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Such activities are pivotal and economically significant to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The stark reality is that some multinational enterprises may hesitate at the prospect of meeting the conditions of these incentives, like substantial investment thresholds and local employment quotas, if the tax benefits do not translate into significant global savings.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: With this in mind, it is imperative for the Government to explore how our incentives might evolve to align with the Pillar 2 regulations of the BEPS framework.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Tax professionals have identified a variety of "BEPS-protected" incentives that comply with the Pillar 2 Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) rules.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, studying these models could provide us with a pathway to adapt and preserve the efficacy of Singapore's tax incentives.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: One viable path forward could be the introduction of Qualified Refundable Tax Credits (QRTCs).

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These credits would be refundable, translating into cash or cash equivalents over a four-year period.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: QRTCs could be strategically directed towards fostering innovation, acting as an enhancement to the current research and development (R&D) tax incentives.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Another possible solution might be the Market Transferable Tax Credit (MTTC), which could function as an investment tax credit.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This credit would bolster sustainability and innovation-driven investments.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Comparable tax credits are in operation in countries like the United Kingdom, Ireland and the United States, where they are treated as income rather than mere tax deductions for GLoBE purposes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Another way to manage the impact of BEPS 2.0 on businesses and investments is to offer more expenditure-related incentives.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For example, Singapore does not offer building allowances unless they meet the conditions for Land Intensification Allowance.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, not all business activities are suited to intensify land use and certain investments do not even qualify for such allowances in the first place, such as clean rooms and even R&D facilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These types of investments are significant and a multi-faceted strategy is crucial to navigate the intricacies introduced by Pillar 2.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A few months back, I did so in the context of the National Productivity Fund, where I stressed how funding for R&D should be clearly directed toward onshore investments and technology adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And in response to Deputy Prime Minister Wong's Budget speech this year, I also specifically touched on how R&D credits being explicitly exempted from the OECD's BEPS 2.0 framework may be exploited as a potential loophole by multinationals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Today, I hope to begin by revisiting the earlier issue of R&D credit loopholes in light of the provisions of this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will then move on to the broader topic of how we plan to continue providing incentives for corporations to locate in Singapore in the wake of a full roll-out of BEPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These amendments set out specific protection associated with intellectual property (IP).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, IP has value and should be appropriately remunerated, a point that I had also made previously on two occasions in this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But in those speeches, I also suggested that there is a tendency for producers of IP to seek protection that would allow them to secure intellectual monopolies and that not every class of IP is deserving of equal protection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the context of this Bill, then my first concern whether the granting of tax concessions for royalties may be justified.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my mind, providing such relief for royalties received by small, independent producers of IP is entirely reasonable, since the amounts involved are typically modest and are likely to constitute a very paltry supplementary income for artists involved in creative work for which we would like very much to encourage in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At this point, I should declare that for many years, my family received royalties associated with several musical compositions by my father, although we have since allowed these to lapse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, it is less clear that tax relief for royalties received at the corporate level, especially in large multinationals, are as easily justifiable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We wish to encourage creativity and innovation and tax exemptions are indeed one way to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, tax incentives offered at the pre-production stage are also an important way to encourage taking on activities such as R&D that carry uncertain payoffs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But royalties received by large corporations occur after the fact and, moreover, are likely to already be subject to corporate taxation in other jurisdictions in which the MNC operates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While it is true that corporations consider the full expected returns from their investments even before embarking on any innovative effort, it is unclear why Singapore should be the jurisdiction that offers such an ex-post write-off, if others do not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A second concern has to do with how the new ARI scheme differs from our existing programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What was the take-up rate of the old ARI and how does the Ministry believe that the new scheme improves on the old?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The mechanism would entail MNC's booking royalties in Singapore for the purposes of qualifying for the tax write-off even when such IP are unrelated to income earned or derived in Singapore, as was previously the case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, then we would merely have facilitated a continued race to the bottom in tax competition, where governments no longer compete to set the lowest tax rate but grant the most lavish R&D tax credits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To get a foretaste of what this could imply it is instructive to look to Ireland.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Due to the overwhelming presence of multinationals booking IP activity and income, often classified as intangibles in Ireland, there has been an increasing divergence in Irish gross domestic product, which measures all activity recorded within the country's borders, and Irish gross national income, which nets out foreign income, including profits sent abroad.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These distortions provide an inaccurate picture of genuine economic progress in that country and, perhaps more critically, provide few jobs or income to Irish citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The artificial, almost comical nature of the phenomenon has even been dubbed leprechaun economics by Nobel Prize winning economist Paul Krugman.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to now move on to the broader context of the Bill, which has to do with our nation's preparedness for the roll-out of BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The onus is thus on us as a nation to prepare our economy, companies and workers to thrive beyond 2024 when agreement comes into fully effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the minimum effective tax rate top-up could result in higher tax revenue, if there is limited flight in existing economic activity, I appreciate that it is of course impossible to fully predict with much precision what the net revenue outcome is going to be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But surely the Ministry has at least outlined revenue implications based on several possible scenarios.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, would the MOF share their homework with this House?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More generally, it would be useful to understand the Government's strategy for and plans to attract and retain foreign investments going forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What does the Government have in mind in terms of these non-tax factors beyond the usual arguments that we offer a skilled workforce, cutting-edge infrastructure and secure investment protections?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, these elements have been unchanging value propositions for quite a while now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if there are changes at the margin that diminish our attractiveness, we must surely offset this by improving something that we have hitherto not yet been able to offer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is important, however, that in doing so we do not compromise the purpose of BEPS and inadvertently become a tool for multinational tax evasion but instead focus on the real intangibles, we can offer as a nation to be an attractive destination for domestic and foreign investment, both into 2024 as well as beyond.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There were a lot going on in both their speeches, so, allow me to take them one by one.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Mark Lee asked for greater clarity on the activities supportable under the ARI scheme and highlighted the importance of refreshing our slate of incentives to align with BEPS 2.0 rules.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These are quite similar to what Assoc Prof Lim had also mentioned.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Allow me to first clarify on the ARI.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There is no change in the scope and intent in terms of what the Government seeks to support under ARI with this enhancement of the approval approach from an agreement-based approach, as I mentioned earlier on, an activities-based approach.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I agree with the Member on the need for clarity over the scope of an approved activity and I wish to assure Members that this new approach will be no different from the approach that we already take for other tax incentives, such as the Development and Expansion Incentive, as I mentioned earlier on.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Given that we aim to attract investments of different profiles and across sectors, the approved activity could vary from project to project.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: EDB will indeed work with companies to define what approved activity would mean in the context of a particular investment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And it is in the interest of both the company as well as the Government for this to be very clearly articulated.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim mentioned this as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It means that we must work even harder to secure Singapore's competitiveness as an investment location.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will hold incentive recipients accountable for their commitments and will not hesitate to amend or withdraw the incentives in the event of breaches, especially if these beaches are wilful ones.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I would also like to thank Members for their suggestions on the different types of incentives that may comply with Pillar 2 of GloBE rules.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Government reviews and refreshes our incentive toolkit on an ongoing basis even as we strengthen our non-incentive advantages, such as the ones that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim had mentioned – our talent pool, our infrastructure, our connectivity.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will take the Members' suggestions into account during these reviews.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Companies take the total cost of the business into account.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They do not look at withholding taxes just in isolation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We consider providing concessionary withholding tax only if it is a necessary to anchor the investment here in Singapore, for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's question, there is actually no change in the intent of the ARI.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The aim is and has always been to anchor economic benefits in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are just making it easier to administer it for companies and that helps to spur investments into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If not for these incentives, there is actually a very real potential that these investments may not be here – in which case, then, there is just no tax to collect in the first place.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I fully agree on a need to strengthen our non-tax propositions and we are working hard on all of the natural advantages that Singapore has, that I think this House had mentioned and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim in the past had also mentioned.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Again, let me reiterate in closing that our tax incentives are really useful tools which our economic agencies like Enterprise Singapore, EDB and the rest, are able to use to attract new investment commitments into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We know for this that will provide intangible economic benefits in the form of value added, in the form of business expenditure.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Ultimately, what we want in this House is good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Among the variety of tools available, tax incentives have been one of the most economically efficient as the tax benefit is premised on the company being profitable.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We have good success in securing substantive business investments and also generating positive economic outcomes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Regardless of their country of origin or size, firms can stand to benefit from tax incentives as long as their investments are able to generate substantive economic outcomes – the ones that I had just mentioned.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I hope that we can continue to anchor more firms and new capabilities in Singapore as the economy grows and as developments, including in METR, as well as BEPS evolve over time.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Through the use of these incentives, there will also be benefits generated to the local ecosystem through the transfer of tech capabilities and skillsets to SMEs, as Mr Mark Lee had mentioned and re-emphasised.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will continue to take in Members' reviews, requests and comments, and review the effectiveness our incentives regularly in order to better influence investors' investment decisions and, ultimately, help Singaporeans and Singapore businesses capture economic value generated through these investments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We look forward to the continued support of this House in our endeavours.
